loci.name: worker-agent-autonomy-reliability-at-scale
loci.one_line: Can a Director spinning up 100+ Worker Agents with minimal human review be production-reliable today, or does current evidence require heavy governance scaffolding before that concurrency target is safe?
loci.rationale: Promoted and validated from the pre-built contradiction graph (cluster autonomy-reliability-fight, decision_relevance: high). Sierra's Agency sandbox post and the Berkeley RDI autonomy-levels paper support feasibility of building the infra (agency-secure-scalable-sandboxes-for-agents-sierra), but the same Berkeley source, plus Shipped by Agents' production-incident framing (structural-risks-of-autonomous-coding-agents-in-production-shipped-by-agents) and the legacy-modernization survey on non-uniform LLM code-understanding, argue reliability-at-scale is unproven and that blast radius from excess permissions is catastrophic and near-instantaneous. The width corpus gestures at the resolution (scale is achievable only with a governance layer) but never cashes out what that layer concretely looks like in terms of permission scoping, kill-switches, and review-escalation triggers for a 100-agent fleet -- which is exactly the architectural answer this whitepaper must give.

opposing_positions.position: Vertically-integrated multi-agent infrastructure (custom Kubernetes-native sandboxing) makes parallel multi-agent software construction at scale feasible today, justifying ambitious concurrency targets.

Frontier agents are not reliably autonomous across long-horizon maintenance; blast radius from excess permissions is catastrophic and near-instant, architectural drift self-reinforces across sessions without hard constraints, and existing security tooling cannot audit agent-generated code at this scale -- human oversight must move up a level, not disappear.

suggested_searches: Shipped by Agents production incident autonomous coding agent blast radius case study
Berkeley RDI autonomy levels framework multi-agent software engineering
Sierra Agency sandbox architecture Kubernetes agent isolation design doc
graduated autonomy levels permission scoping AI coding agent fleet governance

loci.name: pentest-autonomy-regression-vs-mandated-cadence
loci.one_line: Industry adoption data shows full autonomous pentest reliance falling (29%->9% YoY) and no compliance framework accepting a fully-automated AI pentest as sufficient -- does the query's ask for a ~90-min autonomous vuln-sweep-with-auto-patch loop (no human) match what the field is actually converging on, or does it require a named-human-sign-off gate the query didn't ask for?
loci.rationale: automated-penetration-testing-full-autonomy-fell-to-9 cites Cobalt's 2026 Pentesting Pulse Report (455 security leaders): full AI-automation reliance fell from 29% to 9% YoY, with 47% moving to hybrid, 78% reporting false negatives from automated tools; CREST finds only 9% use autonomous agent-based testing; no major compliance framework (PCI DSS 11.4, DORA Art. 27, NCSC CHECK) accepts a fully-automated AI pentest as the whole test, and even XBOW's HackerOne #1 ranking involved human review before posting. This directly contradicts the query's directive for a scheduled, human-free, auto-patch vuln sweep. nobodys-in-the-cockpit-risks-of-autonomous-ai-security-testing (Synack) independently corroborates the risk framing (95% of cURL vuln submissions were invalid AI-agent noise). The corpus never resolves what a defensible ~90-min sweep cadence should look like given this -- it names the regression but doesn't design around it (e.g., OWASP APTS tiering, which parts can safely auto-patch vs. must only auto-flag).

opposing_positions.position: Autonomous, high-frequency, human-free vulnerability sweeps with auto-patch are the target architecture for a continuously-operating software factory, per the query's six-pillar brief.

2026 field data shows the industry actively retreating from full autonomy in security testing (29%->9% YoY), with 78% false-negative rates from automated-only tools and zero compliance frameworks accepting a fully autonomous pentest; OWASP's APTS standard mandates named human sign-off and graduated autonomy tiers as a structural requirement, not an optional add-on.

suggested_searches: OWASP Autonomous Penetration Testing Standard APTS 2026 conformance tiers full text
Cobalt AI and Pentesting Pulse Report 2026 full methodology false negative rate
safe auto-patch vs auto-flag threshold AI vulnerability remediation production case study
CyCognito Horizon3 NodeZero autonomous pentest agent human sign-off workflow

loci.name: probabilistic-skill-sequence-prediction-architecture
loci.one_line: What is the concrete architecture for analyzing an agent's historical trace corpus to probabilistically predict and auto-chain the next Skill/tool call, and how well does it actually perform in production-realistic conditions?
loci.rationale: This sub-question (mapped directly from the query's Pillar 2 'probabilistic sequences' ask) was independently flagged as thin/uncovered after wave 1 in the orchestrator's own coverage-gaps.md and only gap-filled late. The two papers that landed are strong but point in different directions that the width corpus never reconciles: automata-from-agent-traces builds a deterministic FSM substrate (7-43 states, >=0.997 replay fitness, 62% cross-entropy reduction over unigram baseline for next-step prediction, with an early-stopping monitor saving 68% of remaining compute) purely for offline/analytical trace modeling, while act-while-thinking-accelerating-llm-agents-via-pattern-aware-speculative-tool-ex (PASTE) builds a runtime speculative-execution scheduler on mined 'Pattern Tuples' (only 27.8% top-1 accuracy but 93.8% overall hit rate via ranked-candidate speculation) that hides tool latency live. Neither note connects its method to the other, and neither is synthesized into a single actionable architecture for 'predict and chain skills autonomously' as the query demands -- the github-yintonghuoawesome-agent-trajectory survey hub exists in the vault but was never read past the README level.
suggested_searches: agent trajectory mining next-action prediction production deployment case study 2026
FSM automata agent trace skill prediction vs speculative tool execution combined architecture
Agent Workflow Memory AWM baseline comparison skill chaining

loci.name: agent-level-self-termination-decision-logic
loci.one_line: Beyond infra-level VM idle shutdown, what decision logic should an agent itself use to conclude 'I found no issues, I should self-archive' without paging a human -- and how is that distinguished from a false-negative silent failure?
loci.rationale: Flagged thin/uncovered after wave 1 in coverage-gaps.md (Sub-Q13) and only gap-filled late with mostly infra-level sources. idle-shutdown-gemini-enterprise-agent-platform-google-cloud-documentation is explicit that its idle-shutdown mechanism is VM-lifecycle only (defined narrowly as kernel/API activity on a notebook port; CPU usage alone does not reset the timer) and is NOT an agent-logic self-termination decision -- the note itself flags this gap, saying a software-factory would need to 'layer agent-level quiet self-terminate on clean health check logic on top of' it. ai-agent-development-costs-why-sandbox-billing-breaks-blaxel independently documents that average sandbox utilization runs below 20% and idle periods consume up to 48% of energy, which is the economic case for solving this, but no note in the corpus actually specifies the agent-side decision rule (e.g., how a security-sweep agent distinguishes 'clean scan, nothing found' from 'scan silently failed to run' before self-archiving) -- this is the gap between infra plumbing and the pillar-6 behavior the query actually asks for.
suggested_searches: agent self-archive clean health check no issues found self-terminate design pattern
distinguishing silent scan failure from clean negative result autonomous agent
Google ADK Cloudflare long-running agent dormancy wake criteria production

loci.name: consumer-subscription-automation-policy-risk
loci.one_line: If heavy agentic workloads are routed through flat-rate consumer subscriptions (Claude Max, ChatGPT Plus/Pro) via automation harnesses to beat per-token API costs, what are the vendor Terms-of-Service, rate-limiting, and account-suspension risks of doing so at software-factory scale -- and why does the corpus never address this?
loci.rationale: This is an audited absence per the deep-inference directive. The corpus is well-covered on raw subscription-vs-API dollar math (claude-subscription-vs-api-which-is-cheaper-in-2026-real-math-teamorouter explicitly concludes 'CI/CD, background agents, and multi-seat teams exceed subscription session/weekly caps and are economically forced onto metered API billing') and on usage-based pricing shifts (usage-based-ai-pricing-vs-github-copilot-shift), but neither note -- nor any other note in the 110-note corpus -- addresses whether automating a consumer subscription UI/CLI harness for a 5,000-agent software factory violates the vendor's acceptable-use terms, triggers automated abuse detection, or risks account suspension independent of the session-cap economics already documented. The query's Pillar 6 explicitly asks for 'subscription-vs-API token economics for heavy agentic workloads' -- the economics half is answered, the viability/compliance half is silent, and I searched the corpus specifically for ToS/policy/suspension framing and found none.

OpenAI ChatGPT Plus Pro API terms of service automation ban account suspension
automating consumer AI subscription for CI agentic workload legality risk engineering blog

loci.name: agent-skills-context-overhead-magnitude
loci.one_line: Do Agent Skills with progressive disclosure reduce context overhead and token spend as vendor docs claim, or does direct empirical measurement show non-trivial, budgetable token overhead that complicates the cost-optimization pillar?
loci.rationale: Promoted and validated from the pre-built contradiction graph (cluster skills-overhead-fight, decision_relevance: medium). agent-skills-claude-platform-docs and addyosmani's performance-optimization SKILL.md frame Skills + progressive disclosure as reducing context overhead and improving reliability at lower cost; agent-skill-evolution-how-revisions-affect-coding-agents is the only source in the corpus doing direct empirical measurement and finds Skill-body loading carries real, quantified token overhead that progressive disclosure does not fully neutralize, and that Skill size directly trades off against runtime context budget. Both sides agree Skills are net-useful; they disagree on magnitude (negligible vs. material), which is exactly the kind of number a Pillar-6 cost model needs pinned down rather than inherited from vendor marketing.

opposing_positions.position: Encoding SOPs as Agent Skills with progressive disclosure reduces context overhead and token spend versus inline procedural instructions; deterministic Skill sequences improve reliability at lower cost.

Measured independently, Skill-body loading carries real quantified token overhead; adding rules to Skills is not free, progressive disclosure does not fully neutralize that cost, and Skill size directly trades off against runtime context budget.

suggested_searches: Agent Skill token overhead benchmark progressive disclosure measured cost
Claude Agent Skills context budget production case study token count
